definition: A forward-looking assessment of how likely a counterparty is to default on its payment obligations.
core_idea: Credit quality draws on external ratings agencies plus in-house research on key counterparties, and can require multiple layers of analysis since a counterparty's own credit risk depends partly on the credit quality of its clients; a firm also becomes more likely to default once its large trades have moved against it, and less likely once trades have moved in its favor.
key_points: Forward-looking, relevant because many energy contracts run for years.
Ratings agencies provide a baseline; firms often supplement this with in-house research on important counterparties.
Assessment can require layered analysis — a counterparty's credit risk depends on the credit quality of its own clients.
A counterparty's default likelihood shifts with how its large trades have performed: less likely to default if trades favor it, more likely if trades have moved against it.
relationships: One of two components of counterparty credit risk, alongside credit exposure
trading_implications: Monitoring how a major counterparty's other large positions are performing can be an early warning signal for rising default risk, independent of published credit ratings.
